chapters.name: Chapter 1: The CNA path and the basics of safe care

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What a CNA does and how to get certified
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the steps to become a CNA in your state and find your state's official page.
This lesson builds toward: Using your state's official nurse aide registry or health department page, you will list the steps to become a certified nursing assistant in your state, naming the approved program, the competency test and the registry, with the page you checked.
Nursing assistants give basic care and help people with daily living: bathing, dressing, using the toilet, eating, moving and turning. They take vital signs, watch for changes and report them to the nurse. They work under the nurse's direction.
In most states the path has three steps. First, finish a state-approved nurse aide training program. It mixes classroom learning with supervised practice. Second, pass your state's competency test. Third, get listed on your state's nurse aide registry. You must be on the registry to work as a nurse aide in a nursing home.
This course prepares you. It does not give you a certificate. Hours, fees, background checks and test rules differ by state and can change. Check your state's nurse aide registry or health department page, and ask any program you look at whether it is state-approved.
Some programs are free or paid for by an employer, such as a nursing home that hires you while you train. An American Job Center may also help pay for training. Ask before you pay.
Step by step:
- Search the web for your state's name plus "nurse aide registry".
- Open the result from your state's government site (often ending in .gov).
- Write down the steps, the test and any background check rules.
- Write down two state-approved programs near you, and check each one's own page.
Words to know:
- CNA: certified nursing assistant: a nurse aide who passed the state test and is on the state registry.
- Nurse aide registry: the state's official list of nurse aides who may work in nursing homes.
- State-approved program: a training program the state has checked and allowed to train nurse aides.
- Competency test: the state test that checks what you know and what you can do.
Official sources:
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Nursing Assistants and Orderlies
- CareerOneStop: Find an American Job Center
Try it now: Find your state's nurse aide registry or health department page. On paper, write the three steps for your state, the page address, and one rule you did not know (for example about background checks).
You can now list the steps to become a CNA in your state and find the official page that sets the rules.

check.q: Which step comes after you finish a state-approved training program?
check.why: After the program, you pass the state test and then get listed on the registry.

check.q: Where do you check your state's CNA rules?
options: A friend who did it years ago
Your state's nurse aide registry or health department page
Any ad that says "get certified fast"
check.why: The state sets the rules, so its official page is the one to trust.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Clean hands and gloves: stopping the spread of germs
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose when to clean your hands and which way to clean them.
This lesson builds toward: Given a care situation, you will choose when and how to clean your hands and use gloves, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right.
Clean hands are the most important way to stop germs from spreading in a care setting. The people you care for are often older or sick, so germs can hurt them more.
The CDC says health care workers should clean their hands right before touching a patient, after touching a patient or their things, after contact with blood or body fluids, and right after taking off gloves.
Alcohol-based hand sanitizer is the usual choice when your hands do not look dirty. Rub it on all surfaces until your hands are dry, which takes about 20 seconds. Use soap and water when your hands look dirty, before eating and after using the restroom. Scrub every part of your hands and fingers.
Gloves help, but they do not replace clean hands. Use a new pair for each resident, never wash and reuse them, and clean your hands as soon as you take them off. Your program will teach you how to put on and take off gloves, gowns and masks in the right order.
Step by step:
- Clean hands right before you touch a resident.
- Put on gloves if you may touch blood, body fluids or broken skin.
- Take gloves off without touching the outside with bare skin.
- Clean hands right after you take gloves off and before you leave the room.
Words to know:
- Hand hygiene: cleaning your hands with hand sanitizer or soap and water.
- Infection control: the steps health workers take to stop germs from spreading.
- PPE: personal protective equipment: gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection.
Official sources:
- CDC: Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
Try it now: Practice at your own sink. Wash with soap and water, scrubbing palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips and wrists. Then write the four times a CNA must clean hands on a card and keep it for study.
You can now say when a CNA cleans their hands, choose sanitizer or soap and water, and use gloves without skipping clean hands.

check.q: Your hands look dirty after helping a resident. What do you use?
check.why: Soap and water is the choice when hands look dirty.

check.q: You just took off your gloves. What do you do next?
options: Put the gloves in your pocket to reuse
check.why: Gloves do not replace clean hands; clean them right after taking gloves off.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Resident rights, privacy and reporting abuse
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify when a resident's rights or privacy are not respected and say who you report to.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short story about a resident, you will identify whether a resident's rights or privacy are being protected and say what to do if not, including who you would report to.
The people you care for have rights. They choose what to wear and when to rest when they can. They have privacy when they bathe or use the toilet. They are spoken to with respect and called by the name they prefer. Knock, say who you are and explain what you are about to do.
Health information is private. A federal law called HIPAA protects it. Share a resident's information only with the care team who need it for their work. Do not talk about residents in the hallway, at home or on social media, and never post photos of them.
Abuse and neglect can be physical, emotional, sexual or financial, such as taking money. Warning signs include bruises nobody can explain, bed sores, poor hygiene, a person who seems afraid or withdrawn, or a sudden change with their money.
If you see or suspect abuse, tell your nurse or supervisor right away. In many states, nurse aides must report suspected abuse. If someone is in danger right now, call 911. The Long-Term Care Ombudsman in your state also helps residents of nursing homes.
Step by step:
- Knock, say your name and explain what you will do.
- Close the curtain or door for private care.
- Share information only with the care team.
- Report signs of abuse or neglect to the nurse right away.
Words to know:
- HIPAA: a federal law that protects the privacy of people's health information.
- Neglect: not giving a person the care they need, such as food, cleaning or turning.
- Ombudsman: a person who speaks up for residents of nursing homes and helps solve problems.
- Mandated reporter: a worker the law requires to report suspected abuse.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Elder Abuse
- MedlinePlus: Patient Rights
Try it now: Read this made-up story: "A coworker posts a funny photo of Mr. Lee, a resident, on social media, and tells you Mr. Lee's family never visits." Write two problems you see, and what you would do about each.
You can now spot when a resident's rights or privacy are not respected and report it to the right person.

check.q: A friend asks how a resident they know is doing. What do you say?
options: Say you cannot share residents' information
check.why: Health information is private and goes only to the care team.

check.q: You see bruises on a resident that nobody can explain. What do you do?
options: Wait a week to see if they fade
Tell your nurse or supervisor right away
Ask the resident to keep it secret
check.why: Possible abuse is reported to the nurse or supervisor right away.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Daily care, reporting and your test plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Safe daily care: moving, walking and meals
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Put the safety steps for daily care tasks in the right order.
This lesson builds toward: Given a daily care task such as repositioning, helping to walk or serving a meal, you will put the safety steps in the right order, with no step that puts the resident or you at risk.
Every care task starts the same way: clean your hands, say who you are, explain what you will do, give privacy, and check the care plan. Every task ends the same way too: leave the call light in reach, the bed low and locked, and clean your hands.
People who stay in one position too long can get pressure sores, also called bed sores, over bony places like hips, heels and the back. MedlinePlus says to change position about every two hours and keep skin clean and dry. Follow the turning schedule in the care plan.
Falls are a big risk. Keep floors clear, the call light close and the bed low. Make sure the resident has non-slip footwear. Lock wheelchair and bed wheels before a transfer. Use the gait belt and the number of helpers the care plan says.
Protect your own back. Bend your knees, keep the person or object close, and turn with your feet instead of twisting. Never lift a person alone if the plan says two people or a lift. You will practice transfers only in your supervised program.
Step by step:
- Clean hands, say who you are and explain the task.
- Check the care plan and give privacy.
- Lock wheels and lower or raise the bed to a safe height.
- Do the task the way the care plan says, with help if needed.
- Leave the bed low, the call light in reach and clean your hands.
Words to know:
- Activities of daily living (ADLs): everyday self-care: bathing, dressing, eating, using the toilet and moving.
- Care plan: the written plan from the nurse that says what care each resident gets.
- Pressure sore: damaged skin from staying in one position too long, also called a bed sore.
- Gait belt: a strong belt put around a person's waist so a helper can hold on while they walk or move.
- Body mechanics: using your body in safe ways so you do not hurt your back.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Pressure Sores
- MedlinePlus: Falls
Try it now: Write these steps on cards, mix them up, then put them in order: "Lock the wheelchair wheels", "Clean your hands", "Explain what you will do", "Leave the call light in reach", "Check the care plan". Then check your order against the lesson.
You can now put the safety steps for daily care in the right order and explain how they prevent falls, sores and back injuries.

check.q: What do you do before helping a resident move from the bed to a wheelchair?
options: Raise the bed as high as it goes
Lock the wheelchair and bed wheels
check.why: Locked wheels stop the chair or bed from rolling during a transfer.

check.q: The care plan says two people for a transfer, but you are alone. What do you do?
options: Do it alone to save time
Wait for help or ask the nurse
Ask the resident to try alone
Skip the transfer for the day without telling anyone
check.why: Following the plan protects the resident and you; get help or ask the nurse.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Observing, measuring and reporting
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short factual note about a change and report it to the nurse.
This lesson builds toward: Given a made-up resident's chart and a change you notice, you will write a short factual note and report it to the nurse, using what you saw or measured, not guesses.
You see residents more than anyone else, so you are often the first to notice a change. Your job is to observe, record and report. The nurse decides what it means.
The four main vital signs are blood pressure, pulse (heart rate), breathing rate and temperature. You will learn to measure them in your program and practice on classmates under supervision.
Write what you saw, heard or measured, not what you think it means. "Ate half of lunch. Said, 'My stomach hurts.' Holding her stomach." is better than "She seems sick." Write the time and sign your name.
Some changes must be reported right away: new pain, trouble breathing, a fall, a change in how awake or confused someone is, or a big change in a vital sign. When in doubt, tell the nurse.
Step by step:
- Notice the change: what you see, hear or measure.
- Write the facts, the time and your name.
- Report to the nurse right away if it is new or serious.
- Write down that you reported it and to whom.
Words to know:
- Vital signs: measurements of basic body functions: blood pressure, pulse, breathing rate and temperature.
- Objective: facts you can see, hear, measure or count.
- Subjective: what the resident tells you they feel, written in their words.
- Chart: the resident's care record.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Vital Signs
Try it now: Practice only, with a made-up resident: "Ms. Rivera usually walks to breakfast. Today at 8:15 she stayed in bed, said 'I feel dizzy,' and did not eat." Write a three-line factual note and one sentence you would say to the nurse.
You can now write a short factual note about a change you notice and report it to the nurse.

check.q: Which note is written the right way?
options: "10:30. Refused lunch. Said, 'My chest feels tight.'"
check.why: It gives the time, what happened and the resident's own words.

check.q: A resident is suddenly much more confused than usual. What do you do?
options: Wait until the end of your shift
Give them a medicine from the cart
check.why: A sudden change in alertness or confusion is reported to the nurse right away.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting ready for the state test: your study plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a study and test plan with real dates for your state's CNA test.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own calendar, you will build a study and test plan with dates, covering every part of your state's test. Using your state's official nurse aide registry or health department page, you will list the steps to become a certified nursing assistant in your state, naming the approved program, the competency test and the registry, with the page you checked.
In most states the CNA test has two parts: a written test (some states offer it read aloud) and a skills test where you show a few care skills to an evaluator. Your state's registry page or test company page says the exact parts, the skills list and how to sign up.
Use the official candidate handbook if your state has one. It lists the skills, the steps the evaluator watches for and what to bring on test day. Free practice questions from your program help too.
Study a little every day. Practice the skills in class or open lab, where an instructor can watch you. Say each step out loud, including the ones people forget: cleaning hands, giving privacy and leaving the call light in reach.
Plan the practical parts: your ID, how you will get to the test site, child care, and time off work. Write the dates on a calendar.
Step by step:
- Find your state's test parts and candidate handbook on the official page.
- List the skills you need to practice most.
- Set a daily study time and two practice-test dates.
- Write the test date, what to bring and how you will get there.
Words to know:
- Candidate handbook: the official guide from the state or test company that explains the test.
- Evaluator: the person who watches and scores your skills test.
- Skills test: the part of the test where you show care skills step by step.
Official sources:
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Nursing Assistants and Orderlies (How to Become One)
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page CNA study and test plan. Include your state's official page, two approved programs with their cost and start date from their own pages, the test parts, a weekly study schedule with dates, the five skills you will practice most, and one person you will ask when you have a question.
You can now build a study and test plan with dates that covers every part of your state's CNA test.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Official state path No official page, or the steps came from an ad or a friend. Lists the program, test and registry steps from the state's official page, with its address. Also notes the state's background check rules and who to call with questions. Approved programs Programs are missing, or it is not clear they are state-approved. Two programs with cost and start date taken from their own pages, and approval checked. Also lists a free or employer-paid option or help from an American Job Center. Test parts covered Only the written part, or no test parts listed. Lists every part of the state's test and the five skills to practice most. Links each skill to the steps people often forget, like clean hands and privacy. Dated schedule No dates, or one cram session. Weekly study times, two practice-test dates and the test date on a calendar. Also plans test-day needs: ID, transportation, child care and time off. Safety and reporting No person named to report to or ask questions. Names the person to ask or report to, such as the instructor or the nurse. Adds a short practice note written as facts, not guesses. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and check it again.

check.q: Where do you find the exact skills on your state's test?
options: The official candidate handbook or registry page
check.why: The official handbook or registry page lists the skills and what the evaluator checks.

options: Study the night before the test
Daily study, skills practice in class, practice tests with dates
check.why: Regular study, supervised skills practice and dated practice tests cover every part.
